title: Stage I: Task I-B: The Real Story; Task I-C: The Right Story
overview: Chapter 10 completes Egan's account of Stage I by covering Task I-B, the real story, and Task I-C, the right story. Task I-B uses the self-challenge skills of Chapters 6 and 7 to help clients move from a partial account to an accurate picture of their situation, illustrated by Carlos helping Mara after the painful conversation with her father. Egan then gives four principles for helping clients challenge themselves to participate fully: owning problems and opportunities, stating problems as solvable, exploring the problem-maintenance structure, and moving on to the right stage and task. He discusses immediacy, Carkhuff's skill of exploring the helper-client relationship itself, in its relationship-focused and event-focused forms, the situations that call for it, and the wider value of self-challenge. Task I-C introduces the economics of helping and the idea of value, and sets out seven overlapping principles for choosing issues that make a difference: screening, crisis first, most pain, client priorities, manageable sub-problems, general improvement (the spread effect) and benefits over costs, each illustrated by contrasting cases. The chapter ends with the wider use of I-C: value, meaning and making the right choices throughout helping.
objectives: Explain the purpose of Task I-B and how it relates to Tasks I-A and I-C and to the skills of Chapters 6 and 7.
Describe how Carlos helps Mara develop new perspectives as a catalyst in Task I-B.
Discuss the four principles for helping clients challenge themselves to participate fully in helping.
Define immediacy, distinguish relationship-focused and event-focused immediacy, and list situations calling for it.
Explain the wider use of I-B and why Egan believes therapy should be challenging.
Explain Task I-C, the economics of helping and the concept of value.
Discuss each of the seven principles for helping clients work on issues that make a difference, with Egan's illustrations.
Explain screening, the law of the instrument, differential therapeutics and the no-treatment option.
Describe the wider use of I-C in terms of value, meaning and choices, including Boxes 10.1 and 10.2.

sections.heading: Task I-B: The Real Story
sections.detailed:
Place of Task I-B in Stage I. Stage I aims to help clients tell their stories in a way that opens them up to doing something about their concerns. Egan's Figure 10.1 shows three intertwined tasks that work together toward this goal: I-A, the story ("What's going on?"); I-B, the real story ("What's really going on?"); and I-C, the right story ("What should I work on?"). All three help clients explore concerns, gain new perspectives, work on substantial issues and move toward action, leading to ongoing action and problem-managing outcomes. The tasks are not strict steps; they mingle with one another.

Link with Chapters 6 and 7. Egan stresses that Task I-B is not a new set of skills. The communication skills described in Chapters 6 and 7 for inviting clients to challenge themselves are the very substance of Task I-B; the two are, in his phrase, "joined at the hip." In I-B helpers use these skills so that clients can work through blind spots and form new perspectives which in turn lead to new behaviour for managing problems and developing opportunities. Egan therefore tells readers to reread those chapters before going further.

What the real story is. The real story is an accurate picture of the client's problem situation. Egan's example is a client who insists that nothing is ever his fault and that the spouse always causes the trouble; such a version is almost certainly not the real story. A one-sided, self-protective or vague account is common, and I-B is about moving beyond it.

What I-B skills help clients do. Using I-B skills, helpers can help clients: uncover hidden concerns; clarify vague issues; add important details and information that are being left out; explore their hesitancies; see their problems from a more constructive perspective; find strengths and resources they are not using; and spot and explore opportunities that are buried in or masked by problem situations.

Significance. The real story matters because clients cannot manage what they do not see clearly. New perspectives are the bridge between talking about a problem and doing something about it. I-B carries a tone of challenge, but, as the Mara case later shows, the challenge is something clients engage in with the helper's support rather than something done to them.
sections.simple: Task I-B is about getting to the real story, an accurate picture of what is going on. Helpers use the challenging skills of Chapters 6 and 7 so clients can see blind spots, add missing details, find unused strengths and spot hidden opportunities.
keyPoints: Stage I has three intertwined tasks: the story (I-A), the real story (I-B) and the right story (I-C) (Figure 10.1).
I-B asks "What's really going on?"; the real story is an accurate picture of the problem situation.
The self-challenge skills of Chapters 6 and 7 are the essence of I-B.
I-B helps clients uncover hidden concerns, clarify vague issues, add missing details and explore hesitancies.
It also helps them find unused strengths and resources and spot opportunities masked by problems.

sections.heading: Mara and Carlos in I-B
sections.detailed:
Mara after the conversation with her father. Before a conflict-laden talk with her father, Mara had been an excellent participant in counselling; the work was easier because it centred on opportunities such as new career possibilities and a developing relationship with a male friend. The conversation left her shocked and disoriented. Overlooked and new problems surfaced. In later sessions she was depressed, found it hard to talk, felt trapped, was reluctant to consider other possibilities and resisted Carlos's attempts to engage her in self-challenge. A hidden current of resentment at the "cultural captivity" imposed by her parents came up, along with low-grade depression. This was made worse by memories of young people in Iran who seemed "happy and free" and by unacknowledged feelings of vulnerability linked to her car accident. In a sense they were back at square one, without the earlier sense of excitement.

I-B as self-challenge. Egan notes that I-B has an aura of challenge, but it is not something done to clients; clients engage in it with the helper's help. Carlos first notices that Mara has already formed a useful perspective on her own: instead of blaming her discontent on the accident, she sees the accident as a wake-up call.

New perspectives Carlos helps Mara develop. (1) The missing mother: Carlos remarks that Mara never talks about her mother except indirectly as part of "my parents"; she is something of a missing person. Mara realises she does not see her mother as an active agent in her story; her mother is "just there," which may itself be an issue. (2) Doer or endurer: outwardly Mara seems assertive and active, but she tends to put up with personal problems rather than tackle them; she is a doer in some ways and not in others. (3) Living between two cultures: Mara feels culturally adrift, not her own person in either culture, and Carlos wonders aloud how this affects her. She sees her cousins as having adopted the worst of American culture and as narcissistic; her father disapproves but has never said so, and she increasingly wonders what is going on inside him.

(4) Symptoms: Carlos thinks some of her symptoms amount to mild depression but sees no value yet in using the word. He asks whether her insomnia and headaches are signs of health problems or reactions to her concerns. She thinks they are reactions, but decides this may push her to get a physical check-up, which she has not had for years, as she does not want to end up like her father. (5) Duty: Carlos helps her see that she describes herself as very duty-driven; although she does a great deal for her father at work and at home, she feels guilty that she is not caring for him better, and she begins to realise that she resents thinking this way.

How Carlos works. Carlos does not simply tell Mara these things or interpret her words, and he does not use I-B skills to "psych her out." He acts as a catalyst, helping her make discoveries for herself that serve problem management. This is the model for I-B: the helper prompts, the client discovers.
sections.simple: After a painful talk with her father, Mara gets stuck and resists self-challenge. Carlos gently helps her see new things for herself, such as her silence about her mother, her habit of enduring problems and her duty-driven guilt, acting as a catalyst rather than an interpreter.
keyPoints: After the conflict with her father Mara became depressed, felt trapped and resisted self-challenge.
I-B is something clients do with the helper's help, not something done to them.
Carlos highlights her 'missing' mother, her doer-versus-endurer pattern, her cultural drift and her duty-driven guilt.
He asks whether her insomnia and headaches are health problems or reactions to her concerns.
Carlos acts as a catalyst for Mara's own discoveries rather than interpreting or 'psyching her out'.

sections.heading: Help Clients Challenge Themselves to Participate as Fully as Possible: Invite Clients to Own Their Problems and Unused Opportunities
sections.detailed:
Participating fully in helping. Chapter 6 showed many kinds of self-challenge; here the focus is on helping clients get the most out of the helping process itself. Clients benefit when they own the process and take part in it as fully as possible. Even clients with obvious goodwill may struggle to participate for various reasons. Egan offers four principles for helping clients challenge themselves to participate fully and intelligently: own problems and unused opportunities; state problems as solvable; explore the problem-maintenance structure; and move on to the right stage and task. They are principles to use when they benefit clients, not must-do rules.

Lack of ownership. Clients frequently refuse to take responsibility for their problems and missed opportunities, blaming outside forces and other people. Egan quotes L. M. Miller (1984), a counsellor responsible for about 150 young men in a youth prison. What the inmates said when interviewed differed sharply from their files: almost all claimed they did not belong there and gave reasons for their imprisonment unrelated to their own behaviour. One sincerely said he was jailed because the judge had earlier sentenced his look-alike brother; another blamed an uninterested court-appointed lawyer. Egan grants that, given studies on prison life, some of this may be true, but notes that such lack of ownership is common everywhere, especially where blaming someone else is easy.

Three helpers and the business partner. A client's business partner has made a deal on his own; she is alarmed but has done nothing. Helper A reflects anger at his unilateral decision. Helper B reflects anger that her legitimate interests were ignored. Helper C adds that she may have been financially victimised "and you let him get away with it." Challenging clients about ownership means helping them see that they may share some responsibility for creating or at least keeping their problem situations going; only Helper C does this.

Owning opportunities. Opportunities, not just problems, must be seized and owned. Egan cites Wheeler and Janis (1980): opportunities seldom knock loudly, and missing one can be as unfortunate as missing a red-alert warning. Tess and Josh have been fighting bitterly over a cottage left by their late mother. When Josh has a heart attack, Tess knows this is a chance to repair the relationship but keeps putting it off, even though delay makes it harder. In counselling she complains that Josh has said nothing. The counsellor asks what she is doing from her side and finally asks what she would do if someone held a gun to her head and demanded she make it work. Tess realises it is up to her regardless of Josh, admits she is angry with herself and fears he might die while they are still fighting. The counsellor makes clear this is not an assigned task but an opportunity she can still seize.
sections.simple: Clients get more from helping when they take part fully. The first principle is ownership: helping clients see their own share in keeping problems going, and seize opportunities rather than wait for others, as Tess learns with her brother.
keyPoints: Four principles help clients participate fully; they are guidelines, not rules.
Many clients blame others; Miller's prison inmates almost all denied responsibility.
Of three empathic responses, only Helper C ('you let him get away with it') challenges ownership.
Ownership means seeing one's part in creating or perpetuating a problem.
Opportunities must also be owned; Wheeler and Janis warn they rarely knock loudly (Tess and Josh).

sections.heading: Invite Clients to State Their Problems as Solvable
sections.detailed:
Haley's principle. Jay Haley (1976) held that if therapy is to end properly it must begin properly, by negotiating a solvable problem. Egan adds that the same applies to exploring a realistic opportunity.

Unsolvable problem statements. Clients often state problems in a way that cannot be solved, which justifies a "poor-me" attitude and inaction. Egan's illustration is a client who says, in effect, that life is miserable because of the past: indifferent, even hostile parents who, had they been more loving, would have spared the client this mess; the client is the failed product of an unhappy environment. Clients will not speak in such stilted language, but the message is common. Because the past cannot be changed, a problem defined entirely as the result of the past cannot be solved. Such statements tend to invite a sympathetic response about how hard the past was; the client needs to move beyond this view. Clients can, however, change their attitudes to the past and deal with its present consequences.

Solvable problem statements. A solvable or manageable problem is one the client can do something about. Aideen also had a rough childhood with mean parents who did not seem to care when she left. Her restated problem is that she has spent years blaming her parents and does not want to let them off the hook, but she spends a lot of time feeling sorry for herself, sits around doing nothing, makes no friends, does not get involved in the community and takes no steps toward a decent job. This is manageable because it is framed almost entirely in terms of what she does or fails to do. She can stop wasting time blaming parents she cannot change, build self-esteem through constructive action and so stop self-pity, and develop the interpersonal skills and courage to enter relationships more creatively. She can create a different future.

Limits. Not every problem is solvable by the client's direct action. A teenager made miserable by self-centred, squabbling, indifferent parents cannot make them less selfish, stop their fights or make them care more. But he can be helped to cope better by building fuller social opportunities outside the home, developing new perspectives on himself and family life, and being challenged to act internally and externally on his own behalf.
sections.simple: Problems stated purely as the fault of the past cannot be solved and keep clients stuck. Helpers invite clients to restate problems in terms of what they themselves do or fail to do, which opens the way to action, even when others cannot be changed.
keyPoints: Haley: therapy must begin by negotiating a solvable problem.
Unsolvable statements blame the unchangeable past and justify a 'poor-me' stance and inaction.
A solvable problem is one the client can do something about.
Aideen's restatement focuses on her own behaviour, so it becomes manageable.
Where others cannot be changed (the teenager), clients can still learn to cope and act for themselves.

sections.heading: Invite Clients to Explore Their "Problem-Maintenance Structure"
sections.detailed:
Pinsof's idea. Pinsof (1995) emphasises exploring with clients the actions, biology, cognitions, emotions, object relations and self-structures that keep them stuck in their problems. He calls this the "problem-maintenance structure": the set of factors, personal, social, organisational, community and political, that prevents clients from identifying, exploring and finally acting on their problem situations and unused opportunities.

Questions that open it up. Egan gives sample probes: if a client dislikes the way he relates to people, what exactly does he dislike, what keeps that style in place, and what stops him doing something about it? The emphasis moves from describing the problem to understanding what sustains it.

Augustine's case. Augustine, an Egyptian immigrant, was overjoyed to get his green card, but the next two years disappointed him. He drifted from place to place and from one part-time job to another, and his big plans for life in the "land of opportunity" faded. The lifestyle he slipped into made him miserable. A counsellor helped him explore not just what had happened but the factors that kept him locked into a way of life he pretended to like but actually hated. This made him face personal, social and cultural factors he had avoided. Intelligent, personable and a university graduate, he in fact had many unused opportunities.

Restructuring begins in Stage I. The work of helping clients "restructure" self-defeating defences, cognitions, patterns of emotional expression, self-focused and outward-focused behaviour, relationships and approaches to the environment (Egan refers to Magnavita, 2005) starts in Stage I. Exploring what keeps a problem going is the first step toward changing it.
sections.simple: Problems often persist because of a web of personal, social and wider factors. Helpers invite clients to explore what keeps them stuck, as Augustine's counsellor did, so that restructuring self-defeating patterns can begin.
keyPoints: Pinsof's 'problem-maintenance structure' is the set of factors keeping clients stuck.
It includes actions, biology, cognitions, emotions, object relations and self-structures.
Factors may be personal, social, organisational, community and political.
Augustine was helped to see what locked him into a lifestyle he hated.
Restructuring self-defeating patterns (Magnavita) begins in Stage I.

sections.heading: Invite Clients to Move on to the Right Stage and Task of the Helping Process
sections.detailed:
Avoid going round in circles. Egan notes that this point was touched on under probing: there is no reason to keep going over the same issue. Helpers can help clients challenge themselves to move to whatever stage or task will help them most.

What clients can be helped to challenge themselves to do. Egan lists eight shifts: (1) clarify problem situations by describing specific experiences, behaviours and feelings when they are vague or evasive; (2) talk about issues such as problems, opportunities, goals, commitment, strategies, plans and actions when they are reluctant to; (3) develop new perspectives on themselves, others and the world when they would rather cling to distortions; (4) review possibilities, critique them, set goals and commit to reasonable agendas instead of wallowing in problems; (5) look for ways of getting what they want rather than just talking about preferences; (6) spell out specific plans instead of a scattered, hit-or-miss approach to change; (7) persevere in carrying out plans when tempted to give up; and (8) review what is and is not working in their pursuit of change in the outside world.

Summing up. The principle is that clients can be helped to engage more effectively in all the stages and tasks of problem management, both inside sessions and in the changes they pursue in everyday life. Self-challenge is thus not confined to Stage I; it keeps the whole process moving.
sections.simple: Helpers should not let clients circle the same issue. They help clients challenge themselves to move on: get specific, form new perspectives, set goals, plan, persist and review progress.
keyPoints: There is no reason to keep going over the same issue with clients.
Clients can challenge themselves to be specific when vague and to discuss issues they avoid.
They can move from distortions to new perspectives and from wallowing to goals and commitment.
They can make specific plans, persevere and review what is working.
Self-challenge applies to every stage and task, in sessions and in daily life.

sections.heading: Immediacy: Dealing with Issues in the Helping Relationship Itself
sections.detailed:
The session as an interpersonal lab. Many clients have relationship difficulties as a primary or secondary concern. Helping sessions therefore act as an interpersonal laboratory, because key features of a client's interpersonal style show up in the client-helper interaction. Difficulties in everyday relationships tend to be mirrored in the relationship with the helper. A client who is compliant with authority figures may be compliant with the helper, or may swing to the opposite pole and become aggressive and angry. By staying sensitive to the give-and-take of sessions, helpers learn about the client's style (and their own); more importantly, clients learn about their own style. In group counselling the chance to learn is even greater.

Definition. Robert Carkhuff (1969a, 1969b; Carkhuff and Anthony, 1979) gave the name "immediacy" to the package of skills that lets helpers and clients explore their relationship in the service of greater interpersonal competence.

Why it matters. Immediacy is a tool for monitoring and managing the working alliance. Because the quality of the therapy relationship is one of the best predictors of success (Horvath et al., 2011; Norcross and Lambert, 2011), immediacy is important for both helper and client. Clients may or may not have the skill, but helpers certainly should.

Immediacy and ruptures. The skill carries an element of challenge because it is used to repair "ruptures" in the relationship (Safran, Muran and Eubanks-Carter, 2011), defined by Safran and colleagues as a tension or breakdown in the collaborative relationship between patient and therapist.

Two kinds. Egan reviews two forms: relationship-focused immediacy, which looks at the overall relationship ("How are you and I doing?"), and event-focused immediacy, which looks at a particular event in a session ("What's going on between you and me right now?").
sections.simple: Immediacy means helper and client talking openly about their own relationship. Because clients' everyday relationship patterns show up in sessions, this helps them learn about their style, and it helps repair ruptures in the working alliance.
keyPoints: Sessions are an 'interpersonal lab' where clients' relationship styles show up.
Carkhuff named the skills for exploring the helper-client relationship 'immediacy'.
Immediacy monitors and manages the working alliance; relationship quality predicts success.
It is used to repair ruptures: tensions or breakdowns in collaboration (Safran and colleagues).
Two kinds: relationship-focused ('How are we doing?') and event-focused ('What's happening right now?').

sections.heading: Relationship-Focused Immediacy
sections.detailed:
Meaning. General relationship immediacy is the helper's ability to discuss with the client where the two of them stand in their overall relationship, and vice versa. The focus is not on a single incident but on how the relationship has developed and whether it is helping or hindering progress. Ideally, reviewing the ongoing relationship is handled by the feedback systems described earlier in the book.

Example 1: the company counsellor. A 44-year-old woman counsellor in a large company has seen a 36-year-old man every other week for about two months; one of his main problems is his relationship with his female supervisor. Drawing on the feedback they exchange at the end of each session, she observes that they have a good working relationship: mutual respect, the ability to make demands of each other, give-and-take, and anger and impatience that they have worked through. She then asks what their relationship has that might be missing with his supervisor. He replies that she listens to him and his boss does not, but also that he does not listen to his boss at all, thinks she is dumb and conveys this without words. Reviewing the counselling relationship brings the important features of the supervisor relationship into the open.

Example 2: Angie and Weijun. Angie, a 38-year-old trainer in a counsellor-training programme, has not practised the mutual feedback she teaches. She tells Weijun, a 25-year-old trainee, that she wants to talk about their relationship: he seems very careful, speaks slowly as if prepared, has never challenged her, avoids eye contact when talking intimately about himself, and she gives him less feedback than others and has been putting off this talk. She admits it may be partly her imagination but wants to check it out. Egan points out that letting things pile up made matters worse; a feedback system would have prevented this. Weijun admits he too has been afraid and putting it off, and links it to how he relates to authority. Cultural factors play a role: for Weijun, a naturalised American born in China, direct feedback to an authority figure does not come naturally. Yet authority is not the real issue. He thinks her interventions are "unorganized" and that she plays favourites, and he had feared that raising this would jeopardise his place in the programme. Once Angie opens the door, he accepts the challenge.

Who initiates. Immediacy can also be initiated by the client, though many clients hesitate for obvious reasons; few want to take on the leader.
sections.simple: Relationship-focused immediacy is stepping back to discuss how the helping relationship as a whole is going. It can reveal patterns that matter outside counselling, and it works best when regular feedback stops problems piling up.
keyPoints: It discusses where helper and client stand in their overall relationship.
The focus is the relationship's development and whether it helps or hinders progress.
The company counsellor used it to illuminate the client's problems with his supervisor.
Angie and Weijun show the cost of letting issues pile up without a feedback system; culture also played a part.
Clients can initiate immediacy, but many hesitate to challenge the helper.

sections.heading: Event-Focused Immediacy
sections.detailed:
Meaning. Here-and-now immediacy is the helper's ability to discuss with the client what is happening between them at a given moment. The subject is not the overall state of the relationship but a specific interaction or incident.

Example: Agnes. A 43-year-old counsellor at a neighbourhood human services centre is working with Agnes, a recently widowed 49-year-old discussing grief, loneliness and money problems. In one session Agnes withdraws abruptly and the conversation bogs down. The counsellor pauses to look at what is happening between them, notes that the conversation began lively and has become subdued, mentions her own tense shoulders, which happen when she fears she has said something wrong, and says that things seem strained. Agnes hesitantly agrees and explains that she resented an early remark which seemed to imply she was lazy. They discuss it, clear it up and move on. Waiting for the end-of-session feedback would have wasted time.

Carl Rogers and the boring client. Both kinds of immediacy appear in a story told by Carl Rogers, the founder of client-centred therapy. He realised he felt bored every time a particular client came, struggling to stay awake, which was unlike him. As the feeling persisted, he shared it, with difficulty and some embarrassment, saying that when the client talked on and on in a flat tone he found himself bored. The client was jolted and unhappy, then began to talk about the way he spoke and came to see that he talked so uninterestingly because he had never expected anyone really to hear him. Their relationship improved, and Rogers could point out the flatness when he heard it again. Rogers called this "confrontation."

Egan's comments. A feedback system would have prevented the incident. Rogers' self-involving statement was genuine but quite challenging and helped the client move forward at the time, though it did not "solve" the problem. Egan offers another view: someone said that boredom is a self-indictment. Rogers may have been bored because he restricted himself to empathic responding and, on principle, avoided probing, summaries and challenge so as not to take responsibility away from clients. He was a master of empathy, but the story may also show Rogers moving late in his career toward adding the "spice" of probing and challenging (Egan cites Moon, 2007). Egan adds, half-jokingly, that had Rogers used a feedback system we would not have this charming vignette.
sections.simple: Event-focused immediacy deals with what is happening between helper and client right now, as when Agnes's counsellor notices strain and clears up a misunderstanding. Rogers' bored-client story shows its challenging power, though Egan says regular feedback would have prevented the problem.
keyPoints: It discusses a specific interaction or incident in the here and now.
Agnes's counsellor named the strain and cleared up a resented remark at once.
Rogers shared his boredom; the client realised he never expected to be heard.
Rogers called this 'confrontation'; Egan calls it a genuine but challenging self-involving statement.
Egan suggests Rogers' boredom may reflect relying only on empathy; a feedback system would have prevented it.

sections.heading: Situations Calling for Immediacy
sections.detailed:
Knowing when. Part of skilled helping, and of social-emotional intelligence more broadly, is knowing when to use a particular communication skill.

Five situations. Egan lists situations where immediacy can be useful: (1) when a session is directionless and no progress seems to be made; (2) when there is tension between helper and client; (3) when trust seems to be an issue; (4) when diversity, some kind of "social distance," cultural differences or very different interpersonal styles seem to be getting in the way; and (5) when dependency is interfering with helping. His example of dependency is a helper telling the client that the client will not explore an issue without the helper's permission or urging, and that the helper has slipped into the role of permission-giver and nagger.

Caution about purpose. Helpers should know why they are using either form of immediacy. Talking about the relationship is not an end in itself. The relationship is important, but the client's goals are more important. Egan repeats that all these situations could be handled routinely through an ongoing feedback system.
sections.simple: Immediacy is useful when sessions drift, when there is tension, trust problems, cultural or style gaps, or dependency. It should always serve the client's goals, and ongoing feedback can handle most of these issues routinely.
keyPoints: Knowing when to use a skill is part of social-emotional intelligence.
Use immediacy when sessions are directionless or there is tension.
Use it when trust is an issue or diversity/social distance gets in the way.
Use it when dependency interferes (helper becomes 'permission giver and nagger').
Immediacy is not an end in itself; client goals matter more; feedback systems can handle these routinely.

sections.heading: The Wider Use of I-B: Rising to the Challenge
sections.detailed:
From self-examination to self-challenge. Chapter 6 introduced inviting clients to challenge themselves. Ancient Greek wisdom holds that the unexamined life is not worth living; since self-examination leads naturally to self-challenge, Egan says it is equally true that the unchallenged life is not worth living.

Values, not science. These sayings are values and choices people can make, not scientific findings. It is not the helper's job to make choices for clients, but Egan believes it is the helper's job to help clients set the scene so they can make choices. As Stage II will show, clients cannot make reasonable choices for a better future without first understanding the possibilities.

Therapy should be challenging. Egan argues that helping must differ from everyday life if it is to make a difference; therapy itself is, or should be, a challenging experience, and watering it down does clients a disservice. If collaboration is the essence of therapy, clients should know the resources the helper brings: not only the helping model or treatment approach, but the substance of the moves and methods within the problem-management approach.

Implication. The spirit of I-B, inviting self-challenge, is not confined to one task; it is meant to run through the whole of helping and through clients' lives.
sections.simple: Egan argues that an unchallenged life is not worth living. Helpers do not choose for clients, but they set the scene for good choices, keep therapy genuinely challenging, and share openly the methods they bring.
keyPoints: Self-examination leads naturally to self-challenge: 'the unchallenged life is not worth living'.
These are values and choices, not science.
Helpers help clients set the scene for choices rather than choosing for them.
Therapy should be challenging and not watered down.
Collaboration means clients should know the resources and methods the helper brings.

sections.heading: Task I-C: The Right Story — Help Clients Work on Issues That Will Add Value to Their Lives
sections.detailed:
The idea. Many clients bring a range of issues, as Mara does. Helpers should help them choose issues that will make a significant difference. If a client wants to work only on trivial matters or does not want to work at all, it may be better to defer counselling.

Mara's three areas. Carlos asks Mara what matters most and what she would work on if she could choose only one or two things. Three areas emerge. First, she is reactive rather than proactive: apart from a business degree she has done nothing to develop a career, feels she has unused talents, does her assigned work well but adds nothing to the business, and leaves its future to her father although the business could fail given the state of the automotive industry; she is also on automatic pilot with her parents, doing what she is supposed to. Second, she has not come to terms with being an Iranian-American: she has no social life outside family and work, feels a vague taboo about an intimate relationship with a man, does not know what kind of social being she wants to be and hates her "cultural neutrality." Third, she lacks "enthusiasm," probably her way of describing depression. Carlos is hesitant to target the depression directly; she seems depressed because she is going nowhere rather than going nowhere because she is depressed, and he expects it to lift as she makes headway in substantive areas. Mara agrees that it is the opposite of what she had assumed, implying she must work on her work life and social life, with work first.

Feedback. At the start of each session Carlos asks about the impact of the previous one; at the end he asks how the relationship is going, what she has learned and how she will use it between sessions. As a result Mara feels she is getting somewhere.

The economics of helping. Helping is costly financially and psychologically and should not be undertaken lightly. Egan introduces the "economics" of helping, helping clients set priorities, through the term "value." Helpers should ask whether they are adding value through each interaction; clients should be helped to ask whether they are working on the right things and spending time well in and between sessions. The question is not whether helping helps in general, but whether it is working here and is worth it. Clients create value by working on the right things that make a substantive difference, through the quality of their participation, and by making the right decisions. In the end it is their process and they can make it value-added or not.

Two cases. A 41-year-old depressed man has a failing marriage, a boring job, deteriorating relationships, health concerns and a drinking problem; he cannot tackle everything at once, so the blunt questions are where the biggest payoff is, where the limited resources of client and helper should go, and where to start. Andrea, in her mid-30s, referred to a neighbourhood clinic, pours out a history of brutal parents, teenage drug abuse, a poor marriage, unemployment and poverty; the helper can only listen. Where should she start, and how can her investment of time, effort and money bring a reasonable return?
sections.simple: Task I-C helps clients pick the issues that will make the biggest difference. Egan calls this the economics of helping: helping costs time, money and effort, so helper and client must keep asking whether they are adding value and working on the right things.
keyPoints: I-C asks 'What should I work on?' and helps clients choose issues that make a real difference.
If clients want to work only on trivia or not at all, counselling may be deferred.
Mara's priorities: career/proactivity, identity and social life, and 'lack of enthusiasm' (depression).
The 'economics of helping': helping is costly, so priorities and value matter.
Clients create value by working on the right things, participating well and deciding well.

sections.heading: Principles for Helping Clients Work on Issues That Make a Difference
sections.detailed:
Purpose. Egan presents principles for getting value from helping that serve as guidelines for choosing which issues to work on. There are seven, they overlap, and more than one may apply at once.

The seven principles. (1) Determine whether or not helping is called for or should be continued. (2) If there is a crisis, first help the client manage the crisis. (3) Begin with the issue that seems to be causing the client the most pain. (4) Begin with issues the client sees as important and is willing to work on. (5) Begin with some manageable sub-problem of a larger problem situation. (6) Move as quickly as possible to a problem that, if handled, will lead to some kind of general improvement. (7) Focus on a problem for which the benefits will outweigh the costs.

Underlying aim. All the principles try to make clients' first experience of helping rewarding, so that they have the incentive to keep working. They are guidelines, not step-by-step directives. What matters is the outcome: clients working on issues that will make a difference in their lives.

Presentation. For most principles Egan gives a paired case showing the principle violated by one helper and used by another, followed by how Carlos applies it with Mara.
sections.simple: Egan gives seven overlapping guidelines for choosing what to work on: check helping is needed, handle crises first, start with pain, start with what the client values, break problems down, go for issues with spread effect, and weigh costs against benefits.
keyPoints: Seven overlapping principles guide the choice of issues; several can apply at once.
They include screening, crisis first, most pain, client's priorities, manageable sub-problems, general improvement and benefits over costs.
The aim is a rewarding initial experience that gives clients incentive to continue.
They are guidelines, not step-by-step directives.
Most are illustrated by a 'principle violated' and 'principle used' pair.

sections.heading: Determine Whether or Not Helping Is Called For or Should Be Continued
sections.detailed:
Little attention to screening. The literature says relatively little about screening, deciding whether a particular problem or opportunity deserves attention. The reasons are clear: trainees are rightly urged to take clients and their concerns seriously, to adopt an optimistic, hopeful attitude, and to take their profession seriously and believe it makes a difference. So the average counsellor's first impulse is to help no matter what.

The law of the instrument. There is something admirable in this: helpers prize people and set aside the tendency to judge. But helping, like other professions, can suffer from the "law of the instrument": a child given a hammer finds that everything needs hammering. Helpers equipped with models and skills may see every human problem as needing their attention, when in many cases counselling may be useful but cost more than it is worth.

Readiness emerges from dialogue. The helper-client dialogue should determine whether, and how far, the client is ready to invest in change. Change requires work; without incentives clients may start and then trail off, wasting resources. Helmut and Gretchen, mildly dissatisfied with their marriage, seem to want a "psychological pill" and show few incentives to do the work of reinventing the marriage. Further dialogue should explore whether they want to do what counselling requires; the counsellor need not decide unilaterally that it will not work. The decision should come from the dialogue.

Differential therapeutics and no treatment. Frances, Clarkin and Perry (1984), under "differential therapeutics," discussed matching treatments to clients and when no treatment is best. Their no-treatment group includes clients with a history of treatment failure or who get worse in treatment: criminals claiming psychiatric conditions to avoid or reduce punishment; patients with malingering or fictitious illness; chronic non-responders; clients likely to improve on their own; healthy clients with minor chronic problems; and reluctant, resistant clients who use one dodge after another. Helpers and clients must decide case by case, and some may dispute categories, but no treatment deserves serious attention.

Heavy-handed screening. Remarks like "Your concerns are not that serious," "You should manage without help" or "I don't have time for such simple problems," whether said or implied, show disrespect and caricature screening.

Value of stopping. The no-further-treatment option can halt sessions that are going nowhere or are destructive; save time, effort and money; delay help until the client is ready; give a breather to consolidate gains; let clients discover they can manage without treatment; stop helper and client playing games; and motivate clients to find help in daily life. Yet deciding not to treat, or to stop fruitless treatment, is countercultural and hard.

The medical parallel and the helper's stance. Doctors also screen; statistics suggest more than half of people who see doctors have nothing physically wrong, and the best doctors screen while preserving dignity. Effective helpers listen and empathise, picking up clues about commitment without jumping to conclusions, since clients have their own private logic. If problems seem trivial they probe for more substantive issues; if clients resist they challenge and help them work through resistance. But a time may come, perhaps quickly, to judge further effort pointless. It is better to help clients reach this decision themselves; if the helper must call a halt, it should be done in line with basic counselling values.
sections.simple: Not every problem needs counselling. Helpers should screen, through dialogue, whether clients are ready to work, recognise when no treatment or stopping treatment is best, and do this respectfully rather than dismissively.
keyPoints: Screening is neglected because helpers are trained to take all concerns seriously and stay hopeful.
The 'law of the instrument': helpers with skills may see every problem as needing them.
Readiness for change should emerge from dialogue (Helmut and Gretchen).
Frances, Clarkin and Perry's 'differential therapeutics' lists cases where no treatment is best.
Stopping treatment has benefits but is countercultural; screening must preserve dignity and counselling values.

sections.heading: If There Is a Crisis, First Help the Client Manage the Crisis
sections.detailed:
Crises as behavioural emergencies. Phillip Kleespies (2009) compiled a book on "behavioral emergencies"; crises in clients' lives are usually of this kind. He focuses on risk of suicide, violence and victimisation, and also discusses emergency-related crises such as self-injury, personality disorders and substance abuse, for example being caught in the meth trap. Mendenhall (2007), a medical family therapist, describes the crises he defuses in emergency rooms, trauma units and hospital wards.

Crisis intervention and the helping model. Crisis intervention is sometimes seen as a special form of counselling (France, 2005), but it can also be seen as a rapid application of the three stages of helping to the most distressing aspects of a crisis. Egan himself uses a compressed version of the problem-management process to help clients defuse crises.

Zachary: violated and used. Zachary, a second-year student in a four-year counselling doctoral programme, gets drunk and is accused of sexual harassment by a student he met at a party. Knowing he has never harassed anyone, he goes to a trusted faculty member, who asks many questions about his past, his relationships with women and his feelings about the programme. Zachary grows agitated, explodes at the "silly questions" and storms out (principle violated). He goes to a fellow student, who sees his distress, invites him in, listens with few interruptions, sits with him through silence and tears, and slowly "talks him down" until he regains composure. They then contact a friend in student services and hold a counselling and strategy session about the next steps (principle used). The friend's instincts were better: he defused the immediate crisis and helped Zach take the next crisis-management step.

Context matters. In defusing crises it is important to focus on the context in which the crisis occurs (Myer and Moore, 2006). Because the client is often only one of several stakeholders, a client-only focus can be simplistic and ineffective.

Mara's crisis. After the encounter with her father, Mara was in crisis; the world she was building fell apart. Carlos used much empathy to help her work through disappointment, hurt and bewilderment, but also looked for signs of the strength he had seen in her, the foundation of resilience. His best bet was that returning to the work of creating a better future was crucial to managing the crisis.
sections.simple: When a client is in crisis, that comes first. Crisis help is like a fast version of the three helping stages: calm the person, then plan next steps, keeping the wider context and other stakeholders in view.
keyPoints: Crises are usually 'behavioral emergencies' (Kleespies): suicide, violence, victimisation and related risks.
Crisis intervention can be seen as a rapid application of the three stages of helping.
Zachary's faculty member probed his past (violated); his friend listened and calmed him first (used).
Focus on the context; the client is often one of several stakeholders (Myer and Moore).
Carlos combined empathy with a search for Mara's resilience and a return to building her future.

sections.heading: Begin with an Issue That Seems to Be Causing the Client the Most Pain
sections.detailed:
Pain as incentive. Clients often seek help because they are hurting even when not in crisis. Helping them use their hurt as an incentive to work on problems adds value.

Pain and vulnerability. Pain also makes clients vulnerable. If they are open to influence because of it, the helper should seize the opportunity but move cautiously. Pain may also make clients demanding; they cannot see why the helper cannot remove it immediately. Such impatience may be off-putting but needs to be understood. They are like emergency-room patients each seeing themselves as needing immediate attention. Demands for instant relief may reflect a self-centredness that is part of their character and of the wider problem situation. The pain may seem self-inflicted and may eventually need challenging, but pain is still pain; respecting clients includes respecting their vulnerability.

Rob: violated and used. Rob, in his mid-20s, comes in great distress because his wife has left him. The first counsellor judges him impulsive and self-centred and immediately challenges his interpersonal style; Rob seems to listen but does not return (principle violated). A second counsellor notices the same signs but listens carefully to his one-sided story, explores the incident that led to his wife leaving, and rather than adding to his pain focuses on what he wants for the immediate future. When he says he wants his wife back, she notes that his wife would need to be comfortable returning and asks what he could do to make her more inclined to return. His pain becomes the incentive to consider changing even in the short term (principle used). The second helper does not use pain as a club; Rob did not need his nose rubbed in it.

Mara. Mara's sharpest pain came not from her collapsed plans but from her father's "brutal" rejection after her loyalty. She was hurt rather than angry. Carlos asked what sense she could make of what her father did, not to ignore her emotions or excuse him, but to tap the psychological strength he knew she had.
sections.simple: Starting with what hurts most can motivate clients, but pain also makes them vulnerable and impatient. Helpers should respect the pain and use it as a reason to change, not as a weapon, as Rob's second counsellor did.
keyPoints: Clients' pain can be used as an incentive to work on problems.
Pain makes clients vulnerable and sometimes demanding; seize openings but move cautiously.
Even self-inflicted pain is pain; respect includes respecting vulnerability.
Rob's first counsellor challenged too early; the second used his pain to focus on the future.
Carlos invited Mara to make sense of her father's rejection to tap her strength.

sections.heading: Begin with Issues the Client Sees as Important and Is Willing to Work On
sections.detailed:
The client's frame of reference. The search for value starts from the client's frame of reference. The helper may think the client has not picked the most important issues, but working on what matters to the client sends the message that the client's interests matter to the helper.

The woman and her boss: violated and used. A woman believes her boss is sexist: less talented male colleagues get the best assignments and some are promoted. The counsellor explores her family background for "context," concludes she has leftover issues with her father and older brother that colour her view of older men, and pursues this. She feels confused and put down and does not return; he tells himself his hypothesis is confirmed (principle violated). She then consults an older, wise lawyer who handles equal-opportunity cases. He listens, probes for missing details, explains what litigation involves, then helps her explore what she really wants: respect, pay, promotion, revenge, a different boss, better use of her talents, or a non-discriminating employer. Once she names her preferences, they discuss options; litigation is not among them (principle used). The first helper substituted his own agenda and proved somewhat sexist himself; the second accepted her agenda and helped her broaden it, suggesting her situation could be a chance to reset her career, with many firms likely to want someone of her calibre.

Mara. By asking what sense she could make of her father's dismissal, Carlos was testing whether this mattered enough to her to start on now. Mara says it is critical but she could not make sense of it alone and had stopped trying. Carlos offers to be a sounding board, to go slowly and to stop whenever she thinks it is not useful. He asks her to imagine her father having had a real dialogue with her and to describe what would have helped. She says he would have listened more patiently, asked questions to understand her, tried to find out what motivated her even if he disagreed, and not assumed she meant to betray him. Carlos then asks what might have stopped her father doing a more "decent" job, making clear this is to understand, not excuse, him. Mara sees that the aim is not to rehash past misery but to prepare for the next conversation.
sections.simple: Start where the client is. Working on what clients see as important shows respect and keeps them engaged, as the lawyer did and the first counsellor failed to do. Carlos checks that understanding her father matters to Mara before going ahead.
keyPoints: The client's frame of reference is the starting point in the search for value.
Working on the client's priorities signals 'Your interests are important to me'.
The first helper imposed his own agenda (family background); the client left.
The lawyer accepted her agenda, helped her clarify what she wanted and broadened it.
Carlos checked Mara's willingness and helped her prepare for the next conversation with her father.

sections.heading: Begin with Some Manageable Sub-Problem of a Larger Problem Situation
sections.detailed:
Why divide problems. Large, complicated problem situations often stay vague and unmanageable. Breaking a problem into manageable pieces clarifies where value lies, and most large problems can be broken down this way.

Aaron and Ruth: violated. Aaron and Ruth, in their mid-50s, live with their 25-year-old son, who has been diagnosed with schizophrenia. Aaron manages a manufacturing firm in economic trouble; Ruth has a history of panic attacks and chronic anxiety. The marriage is strained, both feel guilty about their son's illness, the son has become abusive at home and is stigmatised by neighbours for his "odd" behaviour, and the parents are stigmatised for "bringing him up wrong." Their counsellor uses a "systems" approach in which everything is related to everything else. Seeking relief but facing ever more complexity, they conclude they lack the resources to cope and drop out.

Aaron and Ruth: used. Some weeks later they see Fiona, a psychiatrist recommended by a friend. She understands the systemic complexity but also their need for respite. She sees the son and prescribes antipsychotic medication, which markedly reduces his odd and abusive behaviour. Though the couple are not actively religious, she arranges a meeting with a rabbi known for ecumenical activism, who links them to an ecumenical group of Jews and Christians starting neighbourhood groups for a "city that cares." Involvement lessens their sense of stigma. They still have many concerns but now have relief and better access to internal and community resources. Fiona targeted two manageable sub-problems: the son's behaviour and the couple's isolation. Some immediate relief put them in a better position for longer-term work. Serious family-systems issues exist, but theories and methods should not take precedence over clients' immediate needs.

Mara. Carlos did not open by asking Mara what she would do next now that her plan had failed; that would dump the whole mess in her lap. Exploring her father's behaviour and contrasting it with what she would have found helpful takes just one piece of the larger situation. Egan asks readers what they would have done in light of this principle.
sections.simple: Big tangled problems overwhelm clients. Breaking them into smaller, manageable parts brings relief and momentum, as Fiona did for Aaron and Ruth, while the systems counsellor's 'everything is connected' approach drove them away.
keyPoints: Large problems stay vague and unmanageable; breaking them down clarifies where value lies.
Aaron and Ruth dropped out of a 'systems' approach that only added complexity.
Fiona targeted two sub-problems: the son's behaviour and the couple's isolation and stigma.
Theories and methods should not take precedence over clients' immediate needs.
Carlos took one piece of Mara's situation rather than dumping the whole mess on her.

sections.heading: Move as Quickly as Possible to a Problem That, If Handled, Will Lead to Some Kind of General Improvement
sections.detailed:
The spread effect. Some problems, once addressed, produce benefits beyond what might be expected. Egan calls this the spread effect, and the principle is to move quickly to problems likely to have it.

Jeff: violated. Jeff, a single carpenter in his late 20s, comes to a community mental-health centre with insomnia, light drug use, alienation from his family, psychosomatic complaints, temptations toward exhibitionism and an intense fear of dogs that sometimes affects his work. The counsellor treats the dog phobia with an evidence-based behaviour-modification method, desensitisation. The fear lessens and many symptoms diminish, but the old symptoms gradually return. The phobia, though significant, is not closely enough related to his main concerns to have a meaningful spread effect.

Jeff: used. His major problems re-emerge; one day, disoriented, he bangs several cars near his job site with his hammer, saying he will get even, and is briefly admitted to a psychiatric ward. The crisis is managed quickly. He talks with a psychiatric social worker, feels good about it and agrees to a few sessions after discharge. The focus turns to his isolation, closely tied to low self-esteem ("Who would want to be my friend?"). He has coped by avoiding close relationships with men and women. Rather than exploring the origins of his isolation, the social worker takes an opportunity-development approach and helps him try mini-experiments in socialisation. As he gets involved with others, his symptoms abate. Lack of human contact was the starting point in the search for value. The experiments also reveal underlying problems: others shy away because of his self-centred, abrasive style. When he repeats his question, the helper says many people would want to be his friend if he were a little more concerned about them and less abrasive, noting he is not abrasive with the helper and asking what is going on.

Mara. Carlos could apply this principle by asking Mara to name one thing she could do that would help her a great deal. Suppose she says she wants the courage to reach out for a different life and not let what happened shut her down; her instinct is to retreat to the safety of her old life, but she wants to be responsible and have the guts not to back down. They then discuss what a "courageous" Mara would look like now, and she notes that a friendship community like the people she met in Iran would make it much easier to stick to her guns.
sections.simple: Pick problems whose solution will improve many other things too (the spread effect). Treating Jeff's dog phobia helped only briefly; working on his isolation improved his symptoms widely.
keyPoints: The spread effect: some problems, once handled, yield wider improvement.
Treating Jeff's dog phobia did not spread because it was not central to his concerns.
The social worker targeted his isolation through mini-experiments in socialisation.
An opportunity-development approach was used rather than exploring origins.
For Mara, building courage and a friendship community could have spread effects.

sections.heading: Focus on a Problem for Which the Benefits Will Outweigh the Costs
sections.detailed:
A call for balance. This principle is not an excuse to avoid difficult problems but a call for balance. If helper and client both put in a great deal of work, there should be a reasonable payoff for both.

Margaret: violated and used. Margaret learns to her horror that her husband Hector is HIV-positive; she and her newborn son are not infected, which softens the shock, but she struggles in her relationship with Hector, who says he got the virus from a "dirty needle" though she never knew he used drugs. The counsellor focuses on "reconstruction of the marital relationship," warning it will be painful because it means examining areas of their lives never discussed. Margaret wants practical help in reorienting herself to her husband and family life, and after three sessions she stops coming (principle violated). Hector's doctor suggests a self-help group for spouses, children and partners of HIV-positive patients. There she learns practically how to relate to someone who is HIV-positive; Hector's absence helps. In the security of the group she understands herself and her needs better and explores mistakes she made with Hector. She does not reconstruct her relationship or personality but learns to live more creatively with herself and her husband, and feels better prepared for future anguish (principle used). She also gets help from sessions she and Hector have with a psychiatric aide.

Lesson. Reconstructing relationships and personality, even if possible, is very costly and chancy; the cost-benefit ratio is out of balance. Again, this may reflect a helper more committed to theory than to client needs. Egan adds that the value-seeking mind-set running through all these principles is second nature to effective helpers.

Box 10.1. Egan lists questions helpers can help clients ask themselves to add value by working on the right things: What problem or opportunity should I really work on? Which issue, if faced, would make a substantial difference? Which has the greatest payoff? Which do I have the will and courage to work on? Which problem, if managed, will take care of others? Which opportunity, if developed, will help with critical problems? Where is the best place to start? If I need to start slowly, where? If I need a boost or quick win, what should I work on?

Mara's cost-benefit analysis. When Mara's instinct is to fade back into her safe old life, she is doing a quick cost-benefit analysis driven by hurt and fear. She knows the power of a cultural mandate in her thinking: do nothing to harm, offend or annoy your parents and always put their needs first. She wants to honour her parents even while questioning this principle. Carlos knows he must help her negotiate with herself.
sections.simple: Work should pay off. Helpers should choose problems where the gains justify the effort, as Margaret's self-help group did and her first counsellor's 'reconstruction' plan did not. Box 10.1 gives clients questions to find the highest-value issues.
keyPoints: A call for balance, not an excuse to avoid hard problems.
Margaret's counsellor aimed at costly 'reconstruction'; she left after three sessions.
A practical self-help group gave her what she needed at reasonable cost.
Theory-driven helpers may put their models above client needs; the value mind-set is second nature to effective helpers.
Box 10.1 lists value-seeking questions; Mara's retreat instinct is a fear-driven cost-benefit analysis.

sections.heading: The Wider Use of I-C: Making the Right Choices
sections.detailed:
Choosing issues. For clients, Task I-C first means choosing which issues to work on. Mara decides that working directly on her depression makes no sense; she believes career work will clear her mind and give her something to strive for, and even help her social life. Career and then social life are most likely the answer to her depression, so working on them has value for her. Value, Egan says, is a cardinal word in therapy, and the wider use of I-C revolves around it.

Value and meaning. In its fullness I-C goes beyond choosing what to work on and contributes to clients' search for meaning. Meaning, as used here, has no basis in science, at least narrowly understood, yet when a client says life is "meaningless" we instinctively understand. Many therapeutic stories are about a lack of meaning, though specifics differ. Things have meaning to the degree that they relate to our values, so the package of beliefs, values, norms, ethics and morality permeates helping, even though its make-up differs from client to client.

Clients create value. Clients do not find value; they create it through their choices and the way they turn those choices into action and life-enhancing outcomes. So I-C is not only about choosing the right issues; it means making the right decisions at every step of helping.

I-B and I-C throughout helping. The spirit of I-B and I-C runs through the whole process and involves decisions based on clients' beliefs and values. At core, both are invitations to self-challenge and a search for value. The principle is to collaborate with the client at every stage and task in adding value: focusing on issues that matter, engaging in substantive self-challenge, setting goals that make a difference, grappling with commitment, making plans that go somewhere and making life-enhancing changes in daily life. If helper and client are merely dabbling in change, they should reset the system or drop the whole thing.

Box 10.2. Broad guidelines in the search for value: help clients focus on issues with payoff potential; maintain a sense of movement and direction; avoid unnecessarily extending problem identification and exploration; help clients move to the stages that will give them most value; remember that clients are making decisions throughout and may benefit from help; and encourage clients to act on what they learn.

Short-term focus. Most therapy is relatively short, perhaps six to ten sessions. Much can be achieved, especially if therapy is designed to help clients "push start" themselves toward more productive ways of thinking, behaving, handling emotions and coping with negative experiences. When clients leave, they should be managing their problems more effectively or be well on the way. There is also some evidence that longer-term therapy can, in some cases, add even more value.
sections.simple: I-C is ultimately about value and meaning. Clients create value through their choices and actions, so helper and client should seek value at every step. Box 10.2 offers guidelines, and even six to ten sessions can 'push start' real change.
keyPoints: For clients, I-C first means choosing which issues to work on (Mara chooses career, then social life).
Value is a cardinal word in therapy; I-C contributes to clients' search for meaning.
Things have meaning as they relate to values; beliefs-values-norms-ethics-morality permeate helping.
Clients create value through choices and action; I-B and I-C run through all stages.
Box 10.2 guidelines; most therapy is 6-10 sessions aimed at helping clients 'push start' themselves.

The Stage I task of helping clients choose issues to work on that will add value and make a real difference ("What should I work on?").
The first Stage I task, helping clients tell their story ("What's going on?"); intertwined with I-B and I-C.
Things clients fail to see about themselves or their situation; I-B skills help clients work through them to form new perspectives.
Fresh, more constructive ways of seeing a problem situation that lead to new problem-managing and opportunity-developing behaviour.
Clients challenging their own views and behaviour with the helper's support; in I-B it is something clients engage in, not something done to them.
Carlos's role with Mara: prompting her to make problem-managing discoveries for herself rather than telling or interpreting.
Clients accepting that they may share responsibility for creating or perpetuating their problems, and taking charge of opportunities.
A problem stated so that the client can do nothing about it, typically blamed wholly on the unchangeable past; it justifies a 'poor-me' stance.
A problem stated largely in terms of what the client does or fails to do, so that the client can act on it.
Pinsof's term for the set of personal, social, organisational, community and political factors that keep clients stuck in their problems.
Helping clients change self-defeating defences, cognitions, emotional patterns, behaviour, relationships and approaches to the environment; it begins in Stage I.
The helping session seen as a setting where clients' everyday interpersonal style shows up and can be learned about.
Carkhuff's term for the skills that let helper and client explore their own relationship in the service of greater interpersonal competence.
The collaborative helper-client relationship; immediacy is a tool for monitoring and managing it.
A tension or breakdown in the collaborative relationship between client and therapist (Safran and colleagues); immediacy helps repair it.
Discussing where helper and client stand in their overall relationship and whether it helps or hinders progress ("How are you and I doing?").
Discussing what is happening between helper and client at a particular moment or in a specific incident ("What's going on between us right now?").
Routine mutual feedback at the start and end of sessions; Egan says it would handle many issues that otherwise require immediacy.
A helper's genuine disclosure of his or her reaction to the client in the moment, such as Rogers' admission of boredom.
The broader competence of which knowing when to use a given communication skill is a part.
Viewing helping as costly in money and effort, so priorities must be set to get the best return.
The worth clients gain by working on the right things, participating well and deciding well; helpers ask whether each interaction adds value.
Deciding whether a given problem situation or opportunity deserves attention, and whether helping is called for at all.
The tendency of a professional armed with a tool to see every problem as needing it, as a child with a hammer finds everything needs hammering.
Frances, Clarkin and Perry's approach of fitting different treatments to different clients, including when no treatment is best.
The judgement that some clients (e.g. malingerers, chronic non-responders, those likely to improve alone) are best not treated.
Interrupting treatment that is fruitless or destructive, to save resources, allow consolidation or wait for readiness.
Kleespies' term covering crises such as risk of suicide, violence and victimisation, self-injury and substance abuse.
Help for clients in crisis; Egan sees it as a rapid application of the three stages of helping to the most distressing aspects.
The result when handling one problem leads to improvements beyond what was expected, in other areas too.
Focusing on building new possibilities, such as mini-experiments in socialisation, rather than on the origins of a problem.
Small real-life steps toward socialising used by Jeff's social worker to reduce his isolation.
The balance between the work and expense of tackling a problem and the payoff expected; it should favour benefits.
In Egan's sense, not scientific: things have meaning to the degree they relate to a person's values; I-C contributes to clients' search for it.
The cluster of personal convictions that permeates helping and differs from client to client.

examples.title: Ownership in a group project
examples.text: A student says, 'My group members never did their part, so our project failed.' A helper who reflects only anger stays at Helper A's level. A Helper C style response might add: 'and you ended up doing nothing about it until the deadline.'

examples.title: Unsolvable vs solvable
examples.text: Unsolvable: 'I can't study because my school never taught me properly.' Solvable: 'I keep blaming my old school and then spend evenings on my phone instead of revising.' The second version points to things the person can change.

examples.title: Event-focused immediacy in practice
examples.text: A counsellor notices a college student going quiet after a remark about attendance and says, 'I noticed you went quiet just now. Did something I said land badly?' This addresses the here-and-now incident instead of waiting.

examples.title: Spread effect
examples.text: Someone stressed about exams, poor sleep and arguments at home starts by fixing a regular sleep routine; better sleep improves mood, study and patience at home, so one change spreads to several problems.

examples.title: Manageable sub-problem
examples.text: Instead of 'sorting out my whole career', a final-year student first works on one piece: updating a CV this week.
