practice.answer: Immediacy is the name Robert Carkhuff gave to the package of skills that lets helper and client explore their own relationship in order to build greater interpersonal competence. Egan treats it as a tool for monitoring and managing the working alliance and for repairing ruptures, and describes two kinds: relationship-focused and event-focused (here-and-now) immediacy.

It is Pinsof's term for the set of factors that keep clients stuck in their problems and stop them identifying, exploring and acting on problem situations and unused opportunities. It covers actions, biology, cognitions, emotions, object relations and self-structures, and includes personal, social, organisational, community and political factors.

The spread effect occurs when handling one problem produces improvements beyond what was expected, in other areas of the client's life. Egan's principle is to move quickly to such problems. Jeff's isolation had this effect when worked on, whereas his dog phobia did not, because it was not central to his concerns.

practice.q: What is meant by the 'law of the instrument'?
practice.answer: It is the tendency of anyone equipped with a tool to see everything as needing it, as a child given a hammer finds everything needs hammering. Egan warns that helpers armed with models and skills may see every human problem as needing counselling, even when its costs outweigh its benefits; hence the need for screening.

practice.q: Define a rupture in the helping relationship.
practice.answer: Safran, Muran and Eubanks-Carter define a rupture as a tension or breakdown in the collaborative relationship between client and therapist. Egan notes that immediacy carries an element of challenge because it is used to repair such ruptures and so protect the working alliance.

It is the term used by Frances, Clarkin and Perry (1984) for fitting different kinds of treatment to different kinds of clients. They also identified when 'no treatment' is the best option, for example for malingerers, chronic non-responders, clients likely to improve on their own and persistently resistant clients.

practice.q: Distinguish between relationship-focused and event-focused immediacy with examples.
practice.answer:
Immediacy, a term from Carkhuff, means helper and client exploring their own relationship. Egan describes two kinds.

Relationship-focused (general relationship) immediacy is the ability to discuss where helper and client stand in their overall relationship, asking in effect 'How are you and I doing?'. It looks at how the relationship has developed and whether it is helping or hindering progress. A company counsellor reviewing session feedback with a man who has trouble with his female supervisor notes their mutual respect and give-and-take, then asks what is missing with his boss; he realises he does not listen to her and conveys that he thinks she is dumb. In another case, trainer Angie raises her concerns about trainee Weijun's caution, which opens up his misgivings about her style.

Event-focused (here-and-now) immediacy deals with what is happening between helper and client at a particular moment, asking 'What's going on between you and me right now?'. When widowed Agnes suddenly withdraws, her counsellor names the strain; Agnes reveals she resented a remark implying laziness, and they clear it up at once. Rogers' disclosure of boredom to a flat-voiced client also shows here-and-now immediacy.

Both serve the client's goals, and Egan stresses that a regular feedback system would handle many of these issues routinely.

practice.q: List the situations that call for immediacy.
practice.answer:
Egan says part of skilled helping, and of social-emotional intelligence, is knowing when to use a given skill. Immediacy can be useful in five situations.

First, when a session is directionless and no progress seems to be made. Second, when there is tension between helper and client. Third, when trust seems to be an issue. Fourth, when diversity, some form of 'social distance', cultural differences or very different interpersonal styles seem to be getting in the way; Weijun's discomfort giving feedback to an authority figure is an example. Fifth, when dependency is interfering with helping, for instance when a client will not explore an issue without the helper's permission and the helper has slipped into being permission-giver and nagger.

Egan adds two cautions. Helpers must know why they are using either form of immediacy, since talking about the relationship is not an end in itself; the relationship matters, but the client's goals matter more. And all these situations could be handled routinely through an ongoing feedback system.

practice.q: Explain how helpers invite clients to state their problems as solvable.
practice.answer:
Jay Haley argued that therapy ends properly only if it begins properly, by negotiating a solvable problem; Egan adds exploring a realistic opportunity.

Clients often state problems as unsolvable, which justifies a 'poor-me' attitude and inaction. A typical version blames present misery entirely on indifferent or hostile parents. Since the past cannot be changed, a problem defined solely by the past cannot be solved, though clients can change their attitudes to it and deal with its present consequences.

A solvable or manageable problem is one the client can do something about. Aideen restates her problem: she blames her parents, feels sorry for herself, sits around, makes no friends, avoids the community and does not look for a decent job. Framed as what she does or fails to do, it becomes manageable: she can stop blaming parents she cannot change, build self-esteem through action and develop interpersonal skills and courage.

Not every problem is solvable by direct action. A teenager cannot change his squabbling, self-centred parents, but he can be helped to cope by building social opportunities outside the home and acting on his own behalf.

practice.q: Explain screening and the no-treatment option in Task I-C.
practice.answer:
The first I-C principle is to determine whether helping is called for or should continue. Screening, deciding whether a problem deserves attention, is neglected because helpers are trained to take all concerns seriously, to be hopeful and to believe in their services. Helping can then suffer from the 'law of the instrument', treating every problem as needing counselling even when costs exceed benefits.

Readiness should emerge from helper-client dialogue. Helmut and Gretchen, mildly dissatisfied and wanting a 'psychological pill', show few incentives for the work needed; dialogue should explore this rather than the counsellor deciding unilaterally.

Frances, Clarkin and Perry's 'differential therapeutics' names groups for whom no treatment may be best: criminals claiming psychiatric conditions, malingerers, chronic non-responders, those likely to improve alone, healthy clients with minor chronic problems and resistant clients who dodge help. Screening must not be heavy-handed or dismissive.

Stopping treatment can end fruitless or destructive sessions, save resources, delay help until the client is ready, allow consolidation, show clients they can cope and motivate them to find help in daily life. It is countercultural and hard, so ideally clients are helped to make the decision themselves, in line with counselling values.

practice.q: Discuss the principle 'If there is a crisis, first help the client manage the crisis'.
practice.answer:
Egan draws on Kleespies, who describes crises as 'behavioral emergencies' such as risk of suicide, violence and victimisation, self-injury and substance abuse, and on Mendenhall's accounts of defusing crises in hospitals. Crisis intervention is sometimes seen as a special form of counselling (France), but Egan sees it as a rapid application of the three stages of helping to the most distressing aspects of the crisis.

Zachary, accused of sexual harassment after a party, goes to a trusted faculty member, who asks about his past and relationships; Zachary explodes and leaves, so the principle is violated. A friend listens, sits with him and 'talks him down', then they consult student services about next steps; the principle is used.

Myer and Moore stress the crisis context: the client is often one of several stakeholders, so a client-only focus can be simplistic.

With Mara, Carlos used empathy for her hurt and bewilderment after her father's rejection but also looked for her strength and resilience, judging that returning to building a better future was key to managing the crisis.

practice.q: Explain the 'economics of helping' and the questions in Box 10.1.
practice.answer:
Egan says helping is expensive financially and psychologically and should not be undertaken lightly. He uses the term 'value' to introduce the economics of helping, which means helping clients set priorities. Helpers ask whether they add value in each interaction; clients ask whether they are working on the right things and using time well in and between sessions. The question is not whether helping helps in general, but whether it is working and worth it here.

Clients create value by working on issues that make a substantive difference, by the quality of their participation and by making the right decisions. Cases such as the 41-year-old man with many problems and Andrea with her story of woe raise the questions of where the biggest payoff lies and where to start.

Box 10.1 lists questions clients can be helped to ask: what they should really work on; which issue would make a substantial difference; which has the greatest payoff; which they have the will and courage to tackle; which problem would take care of others; which opportunity would help with critical problems; where best to start; where to start slowly; and what would give a boost or quick win.

practice.q: What is immediacy? Discuss its types and the situations in which it is useful.
practice.answer:
Introduction. In Chapter 10 Egan discusses immediacy as part of Task I-B, the real story, under the heading of dealing with issues in the helping relationship itself. Many clients have trouble with relationships, either as a main or a secondary concern, so the helping session works as an interpersonal laboratory: the way clients relate in everyday life tends to show up in how they relate to the helper. A client who is compliant with authority may be compliant with the helper, or may swing to anger and aggression. By attending to this give-and-take, helpers learn about the client's style and their own, and clients learn even more about themselves, especially in group settings.

Meaning. Robert Carkhuff named the package of skills that lets helper and client explore their relationship, in the service of greater interpersonal competence, 'immediacy'. Egan sees it as a tool for monitoring and managing the working alliance. Because relationship quality is one of the best predictors of therapy success (Horvath et al.; Norcross and Lambert), the skill matters for both parties; clients may or may not have it, but helpers should. It carries an element of challenge because it is used to repair ruptures, which Safran and colleagues define as tensions or breakdowns in the collaborative relationship.

Relationship-focused immediacy. This is the helper's ability to discuss with the client where they stand in their overall relationship ('How are you and I doing?'). The focus is how the relationship has developed and whether it helps or hinders progress. A company counsellor, reviewing their session feedback, tells a male client they have built respect and give-and-take and asks what their relationship has that his relationship with his female supervisor lacks; he admits he does not listen to his boss and conveys that he thinks she is dumb. In another case, trainer Angie raises her unease about trainee Weijun's carefulness; he admits fear of authority, influenced by cultural background, and then voices his real misgivings about her disorganised interventions and favouritism. Egan notes Angie had let things pile up for lack of a feedback system, and that clients can initiate immediacy but often hesitate.

Event-focused immediacy. Here-and-now immediacy is the ability to discuss what is happening between helper and client at a particular moment ('What's going on between you and me right now?'). When widowed Agnes suddenly withdraws, her counsellor notes the change, mentions her own tension and asks about the strain; Agnes reveals resentment over a remark implying laziness, and they clear it up immediately instead of waiting for end-of-session feedback. Carl Rogers' story combines both kinds: he told a client that his flat, droning talk made him bored; the client realised he spoke that way because he never expected to be heard, and their relationship improved. Rogers called this 'confrontation'. Egan comments that the self-involving statement was genuine but challenging, that a feedback system would have prevented the incident, and that Rogers' boredom may have reflected his reliance on empathy alone.

Situations calling for immediacy. Knowing when to use a skill is part of social-emotional intelligence. Immediacy helps when a session is directionless; when there is tension; when trust is an issue; when diversity, social distance, cultural differences or very different styles get in the way; and when dependency interferes, as when the helper has become permission-giver and nagger.

Conclusion. Immediacy turns the helping relationship into a source of learning and a means of repairing the alliance. Egan cautions that it is not an end in itself: the client's goals matter more than the relationship, helpers should know why they are using it, and an ongoing feedback system can handle many of these situations routinely.

practice.q: Explain Task I-C and the principles for helping clients work on issues that make a difference.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Task I-C, the right story, asks 'What should I work on?'. Many clients, like Mara, have a range of concerns, and helpers must help them choose issues that will make a significant difference. If a client wants to work only on trivia or not at all, counselling may be deferred. Carlos helps Mara identify three areas: her reactive stance toward career and family, her unresolved Iranian-American identity and lack of social life, and her lack of 'enthusiasm', which he expects to lift once she makes progress elsewhere.

Economics of helping and value. Helping is costly financially and psychologically. Egan uses 'value' to introduce the economics of helping: helpers ask whether each interaction adds value; clients ask whether they are working on the right things. Clients create value by choosing substantive issues, participating well and deciding well. The seven principles below overlap, may apply together, are guidelines rather than steps, and aim to make the first experience of helping rewarding.

1. Determine whether helping is called for or should continue. Screening is neglected, and the 'law of the instrument' can make helpers treat every problem as theirs. Readiness should emerge from dialogue (Helmut and Gretchen). Frances, Clarkin and Perry list clients for whom no treatment may be best, and stopping fruitless treatment has benefits, though it must be done respectfully.

2. If there is a crisis, manage it first. Crises are behavioural emergencies (Kleespies); crisis intervention is a rapid use of the three stages. Zachary's faculty member probed his past, while his friend calmed him and planned next steps. Context and other stakeholders matter (Myer and Moore).

3. Begin with the issue causing most pain. Pain is an incentive but also makes clients vulnerable and demanding. Rob's first counsellor challenged his selfishness and lost him; the second focused on what he could do to make his wife want to return, using pain as an incentive, not a club.

4. Begin with issues the client sees as important and is willing to work on. Starting from the client's frame of reference says 'Your interests are important to me'. A counsellor who imposed a family-background hypothesis on a woman with a sexist boss lost her; a lawyer who accepted and broadened her agenda helped her.

5. Begin with a manageable sub-problem. Aaron and Ruth dropped out of a systems approach that added complexity; psychiatrist Fiona targeted their son's behaviour and their isolation, bringing relief. Theories should not override immediate needs.

6. Move quickly to a problem that will bring general improvement. Treating Jeff's dog phobia lacked spread effect; working on his isolation through mini-experiments in socialisation reduced his symptoms widely.

7. Focus on a problem whose benefits outweigh costs. Margaret's counsellor proposed costly 'reconstruction' of her marriage; a practical self-help group helped her live more creatively with her HIV-positive husband.

Conclusion. Box 10.1 gives clients value-seeking questions, such as which issue has the greatest payoff or would take care of other problems. The value mind-set is second nature to effective helpers, and I-C extends into making the right choices throughout helping.

practice.q: Describe Task I-B and the principles for helping clients challenge themselves to participate fully in the helping process.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Stage I helps clients tell their stories in a way that opens them to action, through three intertwined tasks: the story (I-A), the real story (I-B) and the right story (I-C). Task I-B asks 'What's really going on?'. The real story is an accurate picture of the problem situation; a client who says it is never his fault and always his spouse's probably is not telling it.

Nature of I-B. Egan says the self-challenge skills of Chapters 6 and 7 are the essence of I-B. Helpers use them to help clients work through blind spots and form new perspectives that lead to new behaviour. I-B helps clients uncover hidden concerns, clarify vague issues, add missing details, explore hesitancies, see problems more constructively, find unused strengths and spot opportunities masked by problems. It has an aura of challenge, but it is something clients do with the helper's help. With Mara, stuck after her father's rejection, Carlos helps her notice that she never mentions her mother, that she endures problems rather than tackles them, that she feels culturally adrift and that she is duty-driven and resents it. He acts as a catalyst, not an interpreter.

Participating fully. Clients benefit from owning and fully participating in helping, but even well-meaning clients struggle. Egan offers four principles, to be used when they benefit clients.

1. Own problems and unused opportunities. Clients often blame others; Miller found youth prison inmates almost all denied responsibility. Among three empathic responses to a woman whose partner made a deal alone, only the one adding 'you let him get away with it' challenges ownership. Opportunities must also be owned (Wheeler and Janis); Tess realises that repairing her relationship with her ill brother Josh is up to her.

2. State problems as solvable. Haley said therapy must start by negotiating a solvable problem. Problems blamed wholly on the past cannot be solved; Aideen's restatement in terms of her own behaviour makes hers manageable. Where others cannot be changed, clients can still cope and act.

3. Explore the problem-maintenance structure. Pinsof's term covers the personal, social, organisational, community and political factors keeping clients stuck. Augustine's counsellor helped him see what locked him into a lifestyle he hated. Restructuring self-defeating patterns begins in Stage I.

4. Move on to the right stage and task. Helpers avoid circling the same issue and help clients get specific, discuss avoided issues, drop distortions, set goals, seek ways to get what they want, plan specifically, persevere and review progress.

Conclusion. Egan adds immediacy as a further I-B skill and argues that the 'unchallenged life is not worth living': therapy should be challenging, collaborative and transparent about the helper's methods.

practice.q: Discuss the wider use of Tasks I-B and I-C in the helping process.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Egan closes each half of Chapter 10 with a section on the wider use of the task, showing that I-B and I-C are not confined to one moment in Stage I but express a spirit that runs through all of helping.

Wider use of I-B: rising to the challenge. Chapter 6 introduced inviting clients to challenge themselves. Greek wisdom says the unexamined life is not worth living; because self-examination leads naturally to self-challenge, Egan says the unchallenged life is not worth living either. These sayings are values and choices, not science. Helpers should not make choices for clients, but they should help clients set the scene for making choices; clients cannot choose a better future without understanding the possibilities, as Stage II shows. Egan argues that helping must differ from everyday life to make a difference: therapy should be challenging, and watering it down is a disservice. Since collaboration is central, clients should know the resources the helper brings, including the moves and methods of the problem-management approach.

Wider use of I-C: making the right choices. For clients I-C first means choosing what to work on. Mara decides that working directly on depression makes no sense; career, then social life, will give her purpose and probably ease her depression, so they have value for her. Value is a cardinal word in therapy. In its fullness I-C contributes to clients' search for meaning. Meaning here is not scientific, yet clients' stories often concern its absence, and things have meaning as they relate to values. Hence the beliefs-values-norms-ethics-morality package permeates helping, differing from client to client.

Creating value through decisions. Clients do not find value; they create it through choices and by turning choices into action and life-enhancing outcomes. So I-C means making the right decisions at every step. In their core, I-B and I-C are both invitations to self-challenge and a search for value. In every stage and task, helper and client should collaborate in adding value: focusing on issues that matter, engaging in real self-challenge, setting worthwhile goals, facing commitment, making plans that go somewhere and changing everyday life. If they are only dabbling, they should reset the system or stop.

Box 10.2 and short-term work. Box 10.2 advises helpers to focus on issues with payoff potential, maintain movement and direction, avoid dragging out problem exploration, help clients move to the most valuable stages, remember that clients make decisions throughout, and encourage action on learning. Most therapy lasts six to ten sessions, enough to help clients 'push start' themselves toward better ways of thinking, behaving, handling emotions and coping; there is some evidence that longer-term therapy can sometimes add more value.

Conclusion. The wider use of I-B and I-C makes self-challenge and value-seeking the guiding spirit of the whole problem-management process, ensuring that clients leave managing their lives more effectively or well on the way.

practice.q: Explain the principles 'begin with a manageable sub-problem' and 'focus on a problem for which the benefits outweigh the costs'.
practice.answer:
Manageable sub-problem. Large, complicated problems often stay vague and unmanageable; dividing them into smaller pieces clarifies where value lies. Aaron and Ruth, coping with a son with schizophrenia, a strained marriage, anxiety, job pressures and stigma, dropped out of a systems approach in which everything was related to everything. Psychiatrist Fiona targeted two sub-problems: medication reduced the son's abusive behaviour, and links through a rabbi to an ecumenical neighbourhood group reduced their isolation and stigma. Immediate relief prepared them for longer-term work; theories should not take precedence over immediate needs. Carlos likewise took one piece of Mara's situation, her father's behaviour, rather than dumping the whole mess on her.

Benefits outweigh costs. This is a call for balance, not an excuse to avoid hard problems: heavy work should bring a reasonable payoff. Margaret, whose husband Hector is HIV-positive, left a counsellor who proposed painful 'reconstruction' of the marriage. A practical self-help group helped her relate to Hector and understand her own needs. Reconstructing relationships and personality is costly and chancy, and may reflect a helper more devoted to theory than to client needs.

summary: Stage I has three intertwined tasks: the story (I-A), the real story (I-B) and the right story (I-C) (p. 260).
Task I-B uses the self-challenge skills of Chapters 6 and 7 to help clients see blind spots, add missing details, find unused strengths and spot hidden opportunities (pp. 260-261).
Carlos acts as a catalyst for Mara's discoveries about her mother, her enduring style, her cultural drift and her duty-driven guilt (pp. 261-262).
Clients are invited to own their problems and opportunities; Miller's inmates, the three helpers and Tess illustrate this (pp. 262-264).
Problems blamed wholly on the past are unsolvable; restating them as what the client does or fails to do makes them manageable (Haley; Aideen) (pp. 264-265).
Pinsof's problem-maintenance structure covers the factors that keep clients stuck; restructuring begins in Stage I (p. 265).
Clients can be helped to move on to the right stage and task rather than circling the same issue (pp. 265-266).
Immediacy (Carkhuff) explores the helper-client relationship, manages the working alliance and repairs ruptures (p. 266).
Relationship-focused immediacy reviews the overall relationship; event-focused immediacy addresses a here-and-now incident (Agnes; Rogers) (pp. 267-269).
Immediacy helps with directionless sessions, tension, trust, diversity and dependency, but serves client goals; feedback systems handle much of this (p. 269).
The unchallenged life is not worth living; therapy should be challenging and collaborative (pp. 269-270).
Task I-C helps clients choose issues that add value; the economics of helping asks whether helping is worth it here (pp. 270-271).
Seven overlapping principles guide the choice of issues, aiming at a rewarding first experience (pp. 271-272).
Screening matters: beware the law of the instrument; sometimes no treatment or no further treatment is best (pp. 272-274).
Crises come first; crisis intervention is a rapid use of the three stages, attending to context (pp. 274-275).
Start with pain, the client's own priorities and manageable sub-problems, then move to issues with spread effect and favourable cost-benefit ratios (pp. 275-279).
Clients create value and meaning through their choices; I-B and I-C run through all of helping (Boxes 10.1 and 10.2) (pp. 279-281).
